newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil credit curbs not enough - economists.
newsitem.headline: Brazil credit curbs not enough - economists.

text.p: A consumer credit tax hike, aimed at cutting demand to help control a burgeoning trade gap, will not come close to putting Brazil's current account balance of payments woes behind it, economsits said.

"Retailers are very aggressive with sales and promotions so the impact of this tax increase will be very small. This is just a palliative measure," said Andre Carvalho, an economist at Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte-Cindam.

The new restrictions raise a financial tax, known as the IOF, on credit operations to 15 percent from six percent. The increase specifically aims to cut sales of automobiles and electronic goods, imports of which have soared in recent months.
The market had widely expected some credit curbs to slow the trade gap, which is forecast to hit at least $11.0 billion this year.

But economists said the tax, announced by the Central Bank on Friday, was not large enough to control Brazil's ravenous appetite for imports, which totalled $19.3 billion in the first quarter of 1997, 30 percent over the same period last year.

"The Central Bank didn't want to alarm the market. But it is going to have to do more. I expect more measures by the end of this month or in May," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
ING Bank in Brazil listed the following limitations of the tax hike:
* stores that do not borrow from finance companies and finance purchases themselves are exempt from the new rules.
* alternate financing methods, like post-dated checks, are likely to crop up within a few months.
* to reduce the effect of new charges, retailers can simply extend loan periods.
* only 36 percent of cars are sold with consumer financing, which reduces the impact of the higher tax.
* the impact will be less than if the number of installments were reduced because consumers are more interested in the ability to make monthly payments rather than the interest rate.
Although limited in its overall impact, the new tax did offer a further signal to the market that the government has clearly departed from its once-cocky stance over its current account difficulties.
"The latest action by the Central Bank shows they are moving into a more defensive position," said Tina Vandersteel, a fixed-income analyst at JP Morgan in Brazil.

The tax hike follows the Central Bank's decision last month not to lower interest rates for the first time in eight months. The new environment has caused the market to rachet up its long-term interest rate prospects.
Whereas market players once thought monthly interest rates would end the year at about 1.45 percent, they are now looking at a rate of about 1.55 percent.
The Central Bank last week refused to accept offers on longer-dated Central Bank bonds and Treasury notes in what the market viewed as an unwillingness to let markets set long-term rates.
At tomorrow's bond auction, the Central Bank said it would not even offer 182-day paper. Dealers said the bank fears markets may demand too high a rate.
If it is indeed the Central Bank's policy to prevent the markets from setting long-term rates, economists said the plan could backfire.

"Assuming fiscal and forex policies are rigid, interest rates must be allowed to rise, otherwise the authorities will risk losing credibility and reserve loss could result," Vandersteel said in a recent J.P. Morgan report.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5414))
